{{< include /_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

<details class="topic-card" open>
<summary>What the pipe means</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

The tidyverse pipe `%>%` takes the result on the left and passes it into the first argument of the function on the right.

Read this:

```r
data %>% filter(batch == "A")
```

as:

"Take `data`, and then filter rows where batch is A."

This left-to-right reading is the main reason pipes are easier to understand when workflows become longer.

::: {.callout-note}
`%>%` is the tidyverse pipe. Make sure to load the tidyverse with `library(tidyverse)`.
:::

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>Keyboard shortcut for `%>%`</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

In RStudio, you can insert `%>%` with:

- **Windows / Linux**: `Ctrl + Shift + M`
- **Mac**: `Cmd + Shift + M`

This is the fastest way to build pipelines while coding.

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>No pipe vs pipe</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

Start with a very small example so the pattern is clear.

### No pipe

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

x <- c(3.14159, 2.71828, 1.41421)

round(signif(x, 3), 2)
```

### With pipe

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

x <- c(3.14159, 2.71828, 1.41421)

x %>%
  signif(3) %>%
  round(2)
```

Both versions return the same result. The piped version is often easier to read because each step is on its own line.

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>More complex comparison: why pipes help</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

Now compare a realistic multi-step data workflow.

### No pipe (nested calls)

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

tablet_weights <- read_csv("data/tablet_weights.csv")

arrange(
  mutate(
    filter(tablet_weights, batch == "B"),
    pct_target = weight_mg / 500 * 100
  ),
  desc(pct_target)
)
```

### With pipe (step-by-step flow)

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

tablet_weights <- read_csv("data/tablet_weights.csv")

tablet_weights %>%
  filter(batch == "B") %>%
  mutate(pct_target = weight_mg / 500 * 100) %>%
  arrange(desc(pct_target))
```

Both versions are equivalent, but the piped version makes intent much clearer:

1. Start from `capsules`
2. Keep only batch B
3. Add `%` of target column
4. Sort from highest to lowest

That readability is the main motivation for using pipes in tidyverse workflows.

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>How to read a pipeline line by line</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

Use this template mentally:

```r
object %>%
  step_1(...) %>%
  step_2(...) %>%
  step_3(...)
```

Read it as:

- "Take `object`"
- "and then do `step_1`"
- "and then do `step_2`"
- "and then do `step_3`"

If a pipeline feels hard to read, add line breaks so each transformation has its own line.

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>When to avoid piping</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

Pipes are great for transformations, but you can skip them for very short one-step calls.

```r
mean(x)
```

is often clearer than

```r
x %>% mean()
```

Rule of thumb: use pipes when they improve readability across multiple steps.

</div>
</details>
